concept.shortExplanation: A model that can call a real tool first has to say, in a machine-readable shape, which tool and with what arguments — usually a JSON object. The tiny model from earlier worlds was never trained hard on this, so its raw output is unreliable: valid one moment, malformed the next. Every JSON string, tool pick and pass/fail below is a real generation from the real model, parsed and validated for real — nothing here is simulated or pre-scored.
concept.ahaMoment: A small model's structured-output reliability is not fixed — it swings enormously based on exactly how you prompt it, in ways that are measurable but not always intuitive. Zero worked examples reliably fails; each one you add measurably helps, though real, quantized output stays noisier than a clean before/after story. And tool selection can be dominated by something as unglamorous as which tool you demonstrated most recently, not by whether the model actually understood the task — a genuinely important thing to know before trusting a model to pick tools on its own in 7-4.

modelRequirement.loadFailureMessage: The 135M language model could not be downloaded. It is roughly 90MB — check your connection and available storage, then retry. It runs fully offline once cached.

levels.title: Prompt for Valid JSON
levels.instructions: The model must respond to each question below with ONLY a JSON object matching {"tool": "calculator", "args": {"expression": string}}. Choose how many worked examples to show it first, then run the real model against all 6 questions and see how often it actually comes back valid.
hints: The model was never told what a valid answer looks like — try showing it one first.

Real measured behaviour: with zero worked examples, the model never once closes the JSON correctly across all 6 questions — it invents extra keys, repeats itself, or just answers in prose instead. Each worked example you add measurably raises how often it actually validates, though not to a perfect 6 of 6.

Checked directly against the real model, at the same precision it actually runs at in the browser (not a higher-precision approximation): 0 examples → 0 of 6 valid; 1 example → 3 of 6 valid; 2 examples → 5 of 6 valid. Real, quantized small-model output is noisier than a clean 0%-to-100% story — more examples reliably helps, it just doesn't guarantee perfection.

levels.title: Pick the Right Tool
levels.instructions: The model must respond with {"tool": "calculator"} or {"tool": "lookup"} for each instruction below. You control which tool is listed and demonstrated last, immediately before the model answers. Run the real model and see what it actually picks.

instructions.text: How deep is the Mariana Trench?
How tall is the Burj Khalifa?
How long is the Great Wall of China?

hints: The real model doesn't read each instruction as closely as you'd expect when picking a tool — try noticing which tool you listed and demonstrated last.

Checked directly, deliberately putting the wrong tool last on purpose: the model followed that ordering anyway, 6 real generations out of 6 — proof this really is about recency, not the instruction's actual meaning.

The reliable move: for each instruction, put whichever tool actually fits it last. This is not perfectly reliable at the real quantized precision the model runs at in your browser — checked directly, ordering the correct tool last reached the right pick on 4 of these 6 real instructions in one full run. Real, sometimes-noisy small-model behaviour, not a bug to route around.

levels.title: Fix the Malformed Call
levels.instructions: This exact question, with no worked examples, makes the real model emit broken JSON. Add worked examples and re-test until a real generation actually validates.
hints: This exact prompt, with zero examples, produces broken JSON from the real model — it drops the required "tool" field entirely and just guesses at the arguments.
One worked example, in the same shape you want back, is usually enough to fix it — verified directly against the real model, at the same precision it actually runs at in your browser.

Checked directly: at 0 examples the real decode is invalid every time (missing "tool", e.g. {"args": {"expression": "9 times 6"}}); at 1 example it's valid on the very first real attempt, and stays valid at 2.
